THE NEW INSURANCE FRAUD.


READING, Pa., Nov. 27.—Warrants were
issued to-day for the arrest of L. C. B. Yor-
Coy, of Pottstown, and Dr. F. S. Hermann, of
Douglassville, on charge of conspiring to de-
fraud the Prudential Mutual Aid society of
Harrisburg. This is one of the alleged cases
OF fraudulent insurance, obtained on the life
OF Mrs. Reilster of Monocosy, Berks county,
while she was dying with consumption. Wellington and Samuel Shizey, cousins of the
deceased woman, have been arrested on the
same charge. A number of other doctors
will be arrested next week.


FATAL QUARREL.


PITTSBURG, Penn., Nov. 24.—A bloody
encounter occurred at Vernonborough, near
this city, last night between Peter
Skinner and Joe Werle, resulting in Skinner
driving a deep knife in Werle's head with a
knife, from the effect of which he died this
evening at 4 o'clock. Skinner has been ar-
rested.


LOTS OF SUICIDES.


NEW YORK, Nov. 27.—Bernard J. Beck,
formerly in the stationery business, at 1856
William street, killed himself to-day in his
house in Brooklyn.


DETROIT, Nov. 27.—Thanksgiving day
seems to have been adopted in this State as
the favored time to make an exit from this
world of care. A man and wife, at Grand
Haldens, Ingham county, quarrelled about
some trifling matter, when the man left the
house, threatening to shoot himself. No
trace can be found of him, but it is believed
he carried the threat into execution. A well
known farmer, in Mayfield, Lapeer county,
after eating breakfast went to his barn to do
the chores, where shortly after he was found
hanging by the neck and dead. It is sup-
posed a case of dependency over eight

house hanging dead. Domestic difficulties

FOUR IN ONE DAY.


BUFFALO, Nov. 27.—Four railroad ac-
cidents occurred in this vicinity to-day, in-
volving the probable death of six men.
Morris Connell, at round house, boarded
an engine to run it into the round house.
Attempting to reverse it he found it impos-
sible, as the reverse would not work. The
engine crashed into construction train,
killing Frank Kavanagh instantly and &C.
severely injuring John Cosgrove and James
Heiling. While train No. 10, on the
Buffalo, New York &c Philadelphia railroad,
was crossing the trestle this morning, near
Holland, the two rear cars left the track and
went rolling down an embankment about
twenty feet, making complete revolution
and falling into the midst of section hands,
some fifteen in number. The fatally in-
jured are Jeff. Ger of Holland; Joseph Sila-
way, of Protection, and John Lobby, of
Protection. Seriously injured, Jacob Wolf,
of Holland; Martin Wickit, of St. Marys,
Pa.; Samuel L. Look, conductor, and two
others whose names could not be obtained.
The St. Louis express on the New York
Central & Hudson River railway, bound east
with thirteen cars, heavily loaded, met with
an accident at the Forks, seven miles from
the city. Only three sleepers remained
on the track. S. Taylor, of Ithaca, and Miss
Laura Duell, of Oneida, were both
seriously injured. The company attribute
the accident to broken wheel, but it is ru-
mored that the telegraph operator neglected
to have the switch set, and failing to do it
himself when he saw the train coming, ran
away. About 1:30 this morning a collision
occurred at the crossing of the Lake Shore
& Michigan Southern and Buffalo Creek
railways, between an express train going
west and a switch train of coal cars. The
last coach of the passenger train, the sleep-
ing car Getty of Hamilton, was struck in
the center by coal dumps thrown from the
track and badly smashed, but no person was
injured.


BRAVE LITTLE BOY.


JERSEY CITY, Nov. 28.—Mamie and An
ME Arts, respectively seven and five years,
were playing on the ice on the Morris canal
near their home, this afternoon, when the
ice broke and both girls fell into the water.
John Borton, aged 11, witnessing the acci-
dent ran to the assistance of the little girls
and got them both in his arms, but before
reaching shore the youngest was dead.


SHOOTING OF LT. GOV. ROBINSON.


DENVER, Nov. 28.—There seems to be some
mystery about the shooting of Lt. Gov.
Robinson at Robinson's camp last night.

pute about possession of mine there and a
guard had been placed to watch it last night.

mine went to it after dark. The guard not
recognizing them and not hearing the
answer to an inquiry who they were,
fired, he says, into a rock overhead. Gov.
Robinson fell, shot in four places. He is still
living, but the wounds are believed fatal.

ST. LOUIS, June 8. Local preparations for the National Democratic Convention are going rapidly forward, but up to the present time very few out. Also pilgrims have arrived. Judging from the information received at the hotels, the attendance during Convention week will be very large. ALARMING ACCIDENT KINDLING WOOD FACTORY

A singular accident that came near proving fatal
to several persons occurred yesterday at
the kindling wood factory of John Eitel, No.
500 and 531 West Fifty-eighth Street, a
brick building containing machinery
for saving and splitting wood. The Eitel boys were
at work at 10 o'clock when the large
circular saw at it, Mr. Eitel was working, flew
into pieces. The pieces were thrown about with
such force that the men sought refuge under workbench
in one corner of the building. Mr. Eitel made
every effort to throw off the belt that drove the saw
in order to prevent it from becoming entangled with
the shaft. He then saw the shaft was thrown out of
balance and the heavy wood flywheel was
struck and broken into a dozen fragments, which
were flung through the building. One piece
narrowly missed the milling boys; another made
a big hole in the side of the boiler, through which
hot water and steam poured out. Mr. Eitel was
terribly scalded, and the steam flew with such
rapidity that the boys broke into a panic-stricken run
and sprang through a window into the yard and ran for
their lives.

A large piece of iron weighing over five pounds was
thrown through the wall of the building and
landed upon the roof of a two-story tenement
house 800 feet from the factory. It crashed through
the rafters and nearly upset the stove in a room on
the fifth story where Mrs. Joseph was sit-
ting with her infant. She had just moved away
from the lounge when the iron fell. The
tenants in the house were greatly alarmed. Mr.
Eitel was removed to the Roosevelt Hospital. He
was the only person who was injured, but two dogs
that were running about the shop caught the full
force of the stream of hot water and were scalded
almost to death.
